page.title: Queue
page.html:
The Queue page lists tasks with status chips, search, tags, and group chips. The header project filter limits the list and the four status counts. Those counts are totals for the project, not just the rows on screen. The active project chip shows every project except frozen or paused ones; queued tasks waiting on deps/resources (tq.block.*) stay visible.

  • Changing the header project clears the selected group filter (groups belong to a project's task set). The Groups page View in queue link selects the group's project as well.
  • Wait reasons under Status use color: muted for normal waits (resources, exclusive, healthy deps), warn for frozen/paused/service blocks, red when waiting on a dead dependency (failed / interrupted / stopped / missing).
  • Columns hides optional table columns (priority, status, started, finished, resources, description); the choice is kept in this browser.
  • Saved filters remember status, search, and project. Failed today only hides rows on the loaded page whose finish time is today.
  • Selecting rows shows the bulk bar; Select all N matching extends the selection to every task matching the current filters (all pages, up to 5000). Bulk stop and retry send one request (/api/tasks/bulk, /api/tasks/retry-batch).
  • Retry all failed retries the failed query and asks before more than 500. CSV and JSON export download the rows on screen.
  • Running rows show last progress N ago once the % has not moved for a minute, and ⚠ possibly stalled when it has not moved for over 3x the run's usual interval (at least 2 min) — a slow run stays below that (same rule as tq status). A task that exited with one of its negative_exit_codes shows a dashed completed · no badge: a negative result, not a failure.
  • Cap hits show as interrupted with code tq.run.cap (often safe to retry or auto-retried via YAML auto_retry_on_cap). Real crashes show failed / tq.run.nonzero. CLI equivalent: tq retry --project P --status failed,interrupted.
  • Select rows for bulk Retry, Stop, and Re-queue. Force is only offered on queued tasks.
  • With a project selected, Pause project, Block project and Stop All sit in the filter bar. Pause keeps queued tasks waiting while running ones continue (tq pause); Block (freeze) makes the scheduler skip the project entirely.
  • Click a task cell to open the drawer (info, YAML, last five runs). Log opens the bottom panel; its toolbar filters lines by regex (an invalid pattern matches literally), shows only warnings/errors or errors, toggles line wrap, and downloads the log (last 8 MiB). The drawer shows Metrics (TQ_METRIC) sparklines when the task's latest run printed numeric TQ_METRIC values (task-chosen keys — see Metrics (TQ_METRIC); not the same as the 📊 metrics resource-usage modal). Why not running? lists what holds the task back: the scheduler's last block reason, an unmet dependency, a paused project, max_attempts, and for queued tasks a dry-run verdict (same as tq why).
  • Stop waits 5 seconds and shows a toast with Undo before it is sent (a stopped run cannot continue mid-step).
  • Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on macOS) opens the command palette on any page: type to jump to a page, open a task on the loaded queue page in the drawer, or refresh / show shortcuts.
  • Shortcuts while this page is active and focus is not in a field: j / k move the row, / focuses search, r retries and s stops (both ask to confirm), a selects visible rows, Enter opens the drawer, ? toggles the shortcut list, Esc closes the top layer (an open dialog first). Shortcuts are ignored with Ctrl/Alt/Cmd held, and Enter on a focused button activates the button instead of opening the drawer.
  • Shareable URLs keep the section and filters: page (or legacy tab), project, status, q, group, tag, doc. A tq_token in an opened link is saved in the browser and then removed from the address bar, so shared URLs never carry it. Example: /?page=queue&project=omnicard3&status=failed. Browser Back and Forward restore them.
  • A lock contention banner appears when queued tasks wait on a shared resources.locks mutex and the holder's project still has headroom under max_tasks.
  • Queued tasks can also wait on exclusive (blocks all other tasks while it runs) or exclusive_project (blocks only same-project peers). Those show as tq.block.exclusive / tq.block.exclusive_project — Force does not bypass them.
  • Live updates use SSE (/api/events) when the browser supports EventSource; the list refreshes within about a second of status changes. If SSE drops, the page falls back to a slower poll.

general.title: Block project
general.html:
With a project selected, Block project (freeze) stops the scheduler from starting new tasks in that project only. Running tasks continue. Pause is a softer variant.

This is different from the idle FROZEN badge on a running card (no recent log output).

general.title: Force
general.html: Marks the task force_run and re-queues it so soft resource / anti-flap gates are bypassed once. You should see a toast immediately; the task still waits on unmet depends_on, named resources.locks, global exclusive, or per-project exclusive_project. On the Queue page, Force is only offered for queued tasks.

general.title: Groups
general.html:
YAML group: labels tasks for bulk stop/retry and for the group filter chips under status/project on the Queue page. Groups do not change admission priority.

Different from suite (enable/disable all members) — group is for operational batch actions in the UI and CLI.

general.title: Dependencies
general.html:
Deps shows incomplete tasks and their dependency chains (Mode: Active). Attention = blocked/failed/stopped only. All = full graph. Dashed nodes are finished upstream kept for context.

Click a chain chip to isolate a component; focus selection + click drills into a neighborhood; Retry downstream resets a pipe. Pipelines: produce → optional check → consume via depends_on (AND). Fan-in with depends_on_any (OR) appears as edges with kind: any. Nodes may show spawned_by when a parent woke them via on_complete / on_fail.

general.title: Metrics (TQ_METRIC)
general.html:
The Metrics (TQ_METRIC) block in the task drawer (Details → Info) is not a fixed list of daemon fields. It shows numeric keys your task script printed on stdout.

How it works

Any stdout line of the form:

TQ_METRIC {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.124}

is parsed by the runner (and by the master for remote log chunks). Keys are merged into that run’s metric store — last value per key wins. Helpers:

  • Python: tq.metric(epoch=3, loss=0.124) in clients/python/tq_client.py
  • C++: tq::metric({{"epoch", 3.0}, {"loss", 0.124}}) in clients/cpp/tq_client.hpp

What you see in Details

  • Only numeric keys get sparklines (last up to 60 samples per key; at most 8 keys tracked as series).
  • The number next to each sparkline is the latest value for that key.
  • Key names are chosen by the task (loss, val_acc, etl_at_3, …). Taskqueue does not define a standard schema for experiment metrics — ask the owning project what a given key means if it is unclear.

Reserved keys (not task-settable)

KeyMeaning
_seriesInternal time series for sparklines ([timestamp, value] points). Tasks cannot set this via TQ_METRIC.
logAuto-counted log issue chips: errors / warnings / other from stdout classification. Tasks cannot overwrite it.
_progressInternal progress bookkeeping used by the runner.

Not the same as “📊 metrics”

The queue/dashboard 📊 metrics button opens resource usage (CPU %, RAM GiB, VRAM GiB samples from the daemon). That is host sampling, not TQ_METRIC lines.

Tips

  • Prefer small, slowly changing numbers (loss, accuracy, ETA hours). Dumping huge tables into TQ_METRIC wastes disk in the run log and adds little to the sparkline.
  • Progress percent still uses (N%) / tq.progress — that is separate from TQ_METRIC.
  • Full reference: task standards — Structured Metrics.

general.title: Daemon home and port
general.html: Default daemon home is ~/.taskqueue on port 8765. Confirm with tq doctor.

page.title: Dashboard
page.html:
The Dashboard shows CPU, GPU, RAM, queued, and daemon gauges. Each card has a time-series of recent samples (about the last 30 minutes in this browser tab). The line is scaled to that recent range, not to the machine total, so a small move in RAM or VRAM is visible. The caption under the line is the first value, the latest value, and how many minutes the line covers. Queued and running share one chart.

Running cards show #run_id. Log opens the bottom log panel rather than an inline tail. Status and metrics refresh via the shared SSE snapshot (same /api/events feed as Queue); polling is only a fallback when the stream is down.

  • FROZEN badge: no recent stdout on a still-running process. That is not the same as blocking a project.
  • GPU badge: the task requested VRAM (resources.gpu_vram_gib > 0).

page.title: History
page.html:
History lists recent execution attempts. Each row is #run_id for a project/task — use this id when discussing logs, metrics, or a specific failure.

The list loads 20 runs at a time (Load more fetches the next 20). Click History on a row for that task’s prior runs plus duration stats (average / P50 / P95 from completed runs). Metrics opens the resource chart for that run. Re-run (after a confirm) queues the task again with the arguments that run used (subject to the task's overridable_args); tq clone makes a new task from one instead. Click a row to inspect duration, exit status, and link to log search. Filter by project from the header selector. Use the search box to match task id, project, #run_id, error category, or worker id (server-side; works with Load more). / focuses search while this page is active.

Comparing two runs

Click ⇄ Compare on one run row (or the ⇄ button on a dashboard history card), then on a second run. A dialog lists only the fields

that differ: status, exit code, wall time, peak CPU/RAM/VRAM, worker, package hash, command,

effective arguments, environment variable names (values are never stored) and the numeric

metrics. The same data is available from GET /api/runs/<id> and GET /api/runs/diff?a=&b=.

Runs started before the upgrade have no argument/environment snapshot.

GET /api/runs/<id> also returns an anomaly block: peak RAM, peak VRAM or wall time more than 1.5x the p95 of the last 20 completed runs of the same task is listed in anomaly.flags. With fewer than 5 completed earlier runs nothing is flagged.

Re-run with a past run's args. POST /api/runs/<run_id>/rerun re-queues the run's task using the args recorded for that run. The recorded args replace the task's argv tail for one run, so they must stay within the task's overridable_args; otherwise the request is refused with 409 and nothing changes. The task must be in a retryable state. Requires admin scope.

Completed runs that exceeded the anomaly threshold (see GET /api/runs/<id>) show a ⚠ Unusual badge next to their status; hover it for the metric, value and the p95 baseline. GET /api/history returns the same flags as anomalies on each affected run, and the Unusual run alert (Alerts page) fires when such a run finishes.

page.title: Workers
page.html:
Workers lists registered remote machines. Status reflects heartbeat freshness and lease health. Tasks with dispatch: remote prefer online workers; local fallback applies when none match.

Use this tab to confirm a worker is online before debugging remote-only tasks. See WORKER_SETUP.md in the repo for configuration.

page.html:
The Groups tab aggregates tasks by YAML group field. Stop or retry all members of a group from here, or jump to the queue with a group filter applied (View in queue also selects the group's project).

Groups are labels for operations — they do not change scheduler priority. Compare with suite for enable/disable of related tasks.

page.title: Deps tab
page.html:
See the Dependencies topic below for graph modes and pipeline workflow. This tab is the primary place to unblock depends_on chains and retry downstream after fixing an upstream failure.

Pick which task statuses appear with the status checkboxes. Completed, disabled and cancelled start unchecked; unchecking a status removes those tasks (and their edges) from the graph even when something still depends on them. Each node shows its task name, status and project.

Export the graph with GET /api/deps?format=dot (Graphviz DOT; dead edges red, waiting edges dashed) or the default JSON; project and focus apply to both.

The graph is scaled to fill the pane width and scrolls vertically, with scrollbars when it is larger than the pane. The mouse wheel scrolls; Ctrl+wheel or pinch zooms (up to 20×). Drag pans, and Reset view fits the width again.

general.title: Dependencies
general.html:
Deps shows incomplete tasks and their dependency chains (Mode: Active). Attention = blocked/failed/stopped only. All = full graph. Dashed nodes are finished upstream kept for context.

Click a chain chip to isolate a component; focus selection + click drills into a neighborhood; Retry downstream resets a pipe. Pipelines: produce → optional check → consume via depends_on (AND). general.title: Metrics (TQ_METRIC)
general.html:
The Metrics (TQ_METRIC) block in the task drawer (Details → Info) is not a fixed list of daemon fields. It shows numeric keys your task script printed on stdout.

How it works

Any stdout line of the form:

TQ_METRIC {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.124}

is parsed by the runner (and by the master for remote log chunks). Keys are merged into that run’s metric store — last value per key wins. Helpers:

  • Python: tq.metric(epoch=3, loss=0.124) in clients/python/tq_client.py
  • C++: tq::metric({{"epoch", 3.0}, {"loss", 0.124}}) in clients/cpp/tq_client.hpp

What you see in Details

  • Only numeric keys get sparklines (last up to 60 samples per key; at most 8 keys tracked as series).
  • The number next to each sparkline is the latest value for that key.
  • Key names are chosen by the task (loss, val_acc, etl_at_3, …). Taskqueue does not define a standard schema for experiment metrics — ask the owning project what a given key means if it is unclear.

Reserved keys (not task-settable)

KeyMeaning
_seriesInternal time series for sparklines ([timestamp, value] points). Tasks cannot set this via TQ_METRIC.
logAuto-counted log issue chips: errors / warnings / other from stdout classification. Tasks cannot overwrite it.
_progressInternal progress bookkeeping used by the runner.

Not the same as “📊 metrics”

The queue/dashboard 📊 metrics button opens resource usage (CPU %, RAM GiB, VRAM GiB samples from the daemon). That is host sampling, not TQ_METRIC lines.

page.title: Tasks
page.html:
Tasks is one row per project and task from finished runs (completed, failed, interrupted, suspended, stopped). Duration is finish time minus start time.

Average, nearest-rank P50, and P95 use completed runs only. Run count and success rate still cover all terminal statuses (success = share that completed). If a task has no completed samples, duration columns show —.

page.title: Timeline
page.html:
Timeline projects what is likely to run next. It is a forecast, not a replay of past runs.

Each bar is one queued, running, or soon-to-fire cron task. Bars share a forward time axis (now → the selected window: 6h, 24h, 72h, or 7 days). Overlapping bars mean the forecast expects parallel work under global and per-project concurrency limits (max_running_tasks / max_concurrent_tasks, project max_tasks, CPU/RAM/VRAM caps), plus depends_on / exclusive gates.

Duration comes from history when available (task p50), else similar task names in the same project, else the average of known task durations, else a fixed placeholder. Hover a bar for estimate source, lane, and kind. The header shows predicted bunch end (when the last projected bar finishes).

This is advisory: it does not model live host RAM pressure, remote worker binpack, or service probes. The header project filter applies. Scroll horizontally when the chart is wider than the page.

Bars are ordered by projected start. Changing the header project reloads the forecast immediately.

Times are in your local clock: the axis shows HH:MM, each row shows start–end, and the header shows when the queue is expected to drain (~ marks an estimate that is not from the task's own history). The forecast is cached for about 20 s on the server and refreshed from the page at most once every 15 s after the previous request finished (slower after errors; a "stale" note appears if the last refresh failed). Very large queues show the first 300 bars. Prefer the header project filter when possible — scoped forecasts skip other projects' open runs and history. Right-click a bar for Details, Set priority, ±10, Stop, Retry, Force run, Disable and more; click a bar for the details drawer, which also has priority and enable/disable controls.

page.title: Schedule
page.html:
Schedule lists tasks whose YAML contains schedule.cron (five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, evaluated in UTC). Next fire is the next matching minute within 48 hours.

  • Run now re-queues the task.
  • Edit opens that task's YAML.
  • Pause sets enabled: false; a paused row shows Resume instead, which sets it back to enabled: true.
  • New schedule does not insert a task. Put schedule.cron in the project queue YAML and run tq sync. If a row is selected, the button opens that YAML. See the schedule field in task standards.

page.title: Alerts
page.html:
Alerts lists five built-in system events. You cannot create or delete them. Each row has:

  • Active — when on, TaskQueue evaluates / emits the event.
  • Windows popup — when on, a Windows Action Center toast appears. Requires the optional winotify package on the same Python that runs the daemon:
  pip install winotify
  # or: pip install 'taskqueue[toast]'
  # or (project venv): uv sync --extra toast
  tq restart

Toasts are colour-coded like the health light: a 🔴 title prefix and red icon for Any failure (and failed / unknown task-end toasts), 🟠 for Task frozen, Stopped by TaskQueue and Unusual run, 🟢 for No more tasks to run. Toast title names the event and task (for example Task failed: proj/task). The body gives the reason (error label, exit code, last output line) and ends with the running · failed · queued counts. tq doctor and daemon startup warn if Windows popup is on but winotify is missing.

  • Without winotify, alerts still fire: notification bell, in-page toasts when the web UI is open, and Fire count / Last fired on this page. Events are also appended to {TASKQUEUE_HOME}/notify.jsonl with status like alert:any_failure.

Alert history (below the rules) lists every alert that fired, newest first. Click a row for the full detail: error label and code, exit code, attempt, elapsed time, worker, block reason and the last lines of the task log. The notification bell and in-page toasts show the same text (click a toast to open this page). Each alert toasts (and raises a browser notification, if allowed) once per browser: reloading does not repeat it, and alerts that arrived while the page was closed show on the next load. Every alert is also written to the daemon log as a line starting [alert]; suppressed alerts (rule off, cooldown) are logged at debug level under taskqueue.alerts. The structured detail is stored in the detail field of the alert:* event in notify.jsonl; GET /api/notifications?kind=alert returns only alerts.

AlertMeaning
Any failureA run finishes with status failed (any project).
No more tasks to runNothing is queued or running, and at least one run finished recently. Quiet for one hour after it fires.
Task frozenA running task has no stdout and no process CPU for ≥2× frozen_threshold_sec (same condition as the FROZEN badge).
Stopped by TaskQueueAn automated stop (stopped_by=tq), not a human/tq stop. The popup includes why (for example RAM hard limit, wall-clock cap, frozen, dependency invalidated).
Unusual runA run finishes completed but its wall time, peak RAM or peak VRAM is above 1.5x the p95 of the last 20 completed runs of the same task (needs at least 5 earlier runs). The same runs get a ⚠ Unusual badge in History (hover for values). Toast colour: amber.

The sidebar badge counts enabled alerts that are hot now (queue idle, or a currently frozen run). One-shot events (failure, TQ stop) do not keep the badge lit after the toast.

Related: task-end Windows toasts are controlled by config toast_notifications (see WORKER_SETUP); that knob does not gate these system-alert popups.

page.title: Audit
page.html:
Audit lists operator actions: stop, retry, force, enable, priority, freeze, config, project limits, and alert or token changes. The actor is the X-TQ-Operator header when it is set, otherwise web. Heartbeats are not recorded.

Export CSV downloads the rows loaded on the page. This is not the daemon event log. A token secret is never stored in the detail.

API: GET /api/audit accepts actor, action, project (exact match), since / until (ISO timestamps, inclusive), limit (1–2000) and before_id (return events older than that id, for paging). format=csv or format=jsonl returns a server-side export of the filtered events instead of JSON.

Config diff and rollback. A config event records each changed key with its previous and new value (the auth_token is redacted). The Detail column shows the diff and a Roll back button, which restores the previous values and logs a config_rollback event. Keys that were unset before, no longer valid, or secret are skipped. Events recorded before this feature have no stored values and cannot be rolled back. API: POST /api/audit/<id>/rollback (admin scope).

You should see a toast immediately; the task still waits on unmet depends_on, named resources.locks, global exclusive, or per-project exclusive_project. On the Queue page, Force is only offered for queued tasks.

general.title: Groups
general.html:
YAML group: labels tasks for bulk stop/retry and for the group filter chips under status/project on the Queue page. Groups do not change admission priority.

Different from suite (enable/disable all members) — group is for operational batch actions in the UI and CLI.

general.title: Dependencies
general.html:
Deps shows incomplete tasks and their dependency chains (Mode: Active). Attention = blocked/failed/stopped only. All = full graph. Dashed nodes are finished upstream kept for context.

Click a chain chip to isolate a component; focus selection + click drills into a neighborhood; Retry downstream resets a pipe. Pipelines: produce → optional check → consume via depends_on (AND). Fan-in with depends_on_any (OR) appears as edges with kind: any. Nodes may show spawned_by when a parent woke them via on_complete / on_fail.

general.title: Metrics (TQ_METRIC)
general.html:
The Metrics (TQ_METRIC) block in the task drawer (Details → Info) is not a fixed list of daemon fields. It shows numeric keys your task script printed on stdout.

How it works

Any stdout line of the form:

TQ_METRIC {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.124}

is parsed by the runner (and by the master for remote log chunks). Keys are merged into that run’s metric store — last value per key wins. Helpers:

  • Python: tq.metric(epoch=3, loss=0.124) in clients/python/tq_client.py
  • C++: tq::metric({{"epoch", 3.0}, {"loss", 0.124}}) in clients/cpp/tq_client.hpp

What you see in Details

  • Only numeric keys get sparklines (last up to 60 samples per key; at most 8 keys tracked as series).
  • The number next to each sparkline is the latest value for that key.
  • Key names are chosen by the task (loss, val_acc, etl_at_3, …). Taskqueue does not define a standard schema for experiment metrics — ask the owning project what a given key means if it is unclear.

Reserved keys (not task-settable)

KeyMeaning
_seriesInternal time series for sparklines ([timestamp, value] points). Tasks cannot set this via TQ_METRIC.
logAuto-counted log issue chips: errors / warnings / other from stdout classification. Tasks cannot overwrite it.
_progressInternal progress bookkeeping used by the runner.

Not the same as “📊 metrics”

The queue/dashboard 📊 metrics button opens resource usage (CPU %, RAM GiB, VRAM GiB samples from the daemon). That is host sampling, not TQ_METRIC lines.

Tips

  • Prefer small, slowly changing numbers (loss, accuracy, ETA hours). Dumping huge tables into TQ_METRIC wastes disk in the run log and adds little to the sparkline.
  • Progress percent still uses (N%) / tq.progress — that is separate from TQ_METRIC.
  • Full reference: task standards — Structured Metrics.

general.title: Daemon home and port
general.html: Default daemon home is ~/.taskqueue on port 8765. Confirm with tq doctor.

page.title: API tokens
page.html:
API creates a scoped token. The secret (tq_live_…) is shown once. The database stores a SHA-256 hash and a prefix.

  • read — GET
  • write — GET plus task changes (stop, retry, force, enable, priority, freeze, YAML; many tasks at once via POST /api/tasks/bulk)
  • admin — config, project limits, alerts, and token create or revoke, plus write

The optional Projects field (comma separated) limits a read or write token to those projects. Such a token may only read the queue, history and audit lists with a project filter naming an allowed project; every other route returns 403. It cannot be combined with admin. See security.

The daemon auth_token remains an admin credential. Workers and the master lease keep using that token, not a scoped one. Revoke marks the token revoked. Loopback browsers skip the token check.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer tq_live_…" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/status

Route list: /api/docs.

general.title: Block project
general.html:
With a project selected, Block project (freeze) stops the scheduler from starting new tasks in that project only. Running tasks continue. Pause is a softer variant.

This is different from the idle FROZEN badge on a running card (no recent log output).

page.title: Config
page.html:
Config edits live daemon settings: CPU/GPU/RAM soft limits, max_running_tasks, graceful stop seconds, and frozen threshold (idle detection).

Per-project rows set max concurrent tasks, min tasks (slots held back from other projects while this project has queued work and fewer running; only meaningful with a global max_running_tasks; force bypasses), and RAM/VRAM caps. Changes apply on save; running tasks are not restarted automatically.

See scheduler.md for how admission uses these limits.
